approachQuestion.prompt:
Sorting trays

An array p is a permutation of the integers 0 through n-1. Partition it into nonempty contiguous trays. Each tray is sorted independently and the sorted trays are concatenated without reordering trays. Return the maximum possible number of trays for which the concatenation equals [0,1,...,n-1].

Example 1: p=[1,0,2,4,3] → 3, using [1,0], [2], [4,3].
Example 2: p=[2,1,0] → 1.
Example 3: p=[] → 0.

Constraints: 0 ≤ n ≤ 200000; every integer 0..n-1 appears exactly once. You return only the maximum count, without actually sorting any tray. Input is read-only. Return only the stated scalar result. All arithmetic and comparisons use constant-time exact 64-bit operations; all intermediate values fit.

options.text: Scan with the largest value seen. Whenever that maximum equals the current zero-based index i, end a tray and increment the count.
options.feedback: A prefix of i+1 distinct nonnegative permutation values has maximum i exactly when it contains all values 0..i. That is precisely a safe cut: no smaller value is stranded later. Every safe boundary may be used simultaneously, so taking all of them maximizes the count.

options.text: End a tray whenever the current value equals its index.
options.feedback: A safe boundary need not have the boundary value at its last position. For [1,0], the prefix maximum at index 1 is 1 and one tray is valid, but neither entry equals its index.

options.text: End a tray at each adjacent ascent, and always end the final tray.
options.feedback: A local ascent does not imply that all smaller values are in the prefix. For [1,2,0], an ascent after 1 would split the needed value 0 into a later tray, making a globally sorted concatenation impossible.

options.text: Maintain the same running maximum but save a Boolean marker for every safe boundary in a length-n array, then count the marked entries.
options.feedback: The safe-boundary test is correct. Saving every marker adds removable memory because the result asks only for their count.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze only the revealed frontier method, regardless of your previous choice. Use exactly the frontier method above as iterative scans with scalar indices, counters and accumulators. Do not copy the input and do not store a decision list. Let n be the number of input records or positions. Choose the tightest standard worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair.
constraints: Input and returned scalar are excluded. All other live storage, including copying and any call stack, is counted. No hashing or expected-time operations are used.

feedback.reason: One running maximum identifies each legal tray boundary in a single scan.

messages.text: The method stores no per-item history or copied input.
The scans do not restart for each item.
In the worst case every input item can affect the answer.

details: The maximum update and equality test perform constant work per permutation entry, giving O(n) total. Only the running maximum, index, and tray count remain live, so no prefix array contributes auxiliary space.
“Time O(n), auxiliary space O(n)”: The method stores no per-item history or copied input.
“Time O(n²), auxiliary space O(1)”: The scans do not restart for each item.
“Time O(1), auxiliary space O(1)”: In the worst case every input item can affect the answer.
